newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian parties edge towards power-sharing deal.
newsitem.headline: Indian parties edge towards power-sharing deal.

text.p: India's two-week political crisis eased after the United Front coalition agreed to consider replacing its defeated leader, caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, to avoid snap elections.

The coalition's policy-making Steering Committee retreated on Sunday from its earlier hard line that it would not bow to a demand by the rival Congress party to drop Deve Gowda as United Front leader before a new government could be forged.

"I am not saying that a change in leadership is ruled out," a senior United Front official told reporters after the Steering Committee meeting. "Till yesterday, we were saying that a change in leadership is not negotiable."

Deve Gowda, who had vehemently opposed stepping down, said he would abide by the wishes of the Steering Committee, set to meet on Thursday to take a final decision, coalition spokesman Jaipal Reddy said.

Deve Gowda lost a vote of confidence in the lower house of parliament on Friday but stayed as caretaker prime minister until a new government was set up, either through the formation of a new cabinet or mid-term elections.

Four regional parties in the United Front -- two from Tamil Nadu state, one from Andhra Pradesh and the fourth from Assam -- made clear they wanted to sidestep fresh polls and Reddy said after the Steering Committee: "The general view was elections should be avoided."

Deve Gowda had repeatedly said there was no alternative to elections as Congress had withdrawn support from the United Front coalition. No single political formation controls a majority in the 542-member lower house.

Many deputies in both the 15-party United Front and Congress believe that new elections would probably strengthen their common political foe, the right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Congress president Sitaram Kesri provoked the political crisis on March 30 when he told President Shankar Dayal Sharma that he was withdrawing his party's support for Deve Gowda.
He accused his rival of trying to sideline Congress, which had backed the minority government while staying out of the cabinet, and he wrote to the president staking a claim to form a new government.

But Kesri, under pressure from deputies opposed to snap polls, said on Saturday that he did not want to lead a new government and was willing to support the United Front provided it abandoned Deve Gowda.
Congress parliamentary deputy and former minister Rajesh Pilot said he was optimistic that the two groups would sink their differences and hammer out a compromise very soon.
"I think we can find a solution even as early as the next two or three days," Pilot told Reuters Television.
The senior United Front official said the coalition was asking the policy-making Congress Working Committee (CWC), set to meet on Monday, to retract Kesri's claim to form a government.
"The CWC must make the formal offer. They must convey their latest decision to the president which means a reversal of the earlier decision," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
